_comment: Least-privilege Elasticsearch role for the audit service.
Apply, then mint a scoped API key for ES_API_KEY:
PUT  _security/role/audit_service          <- the 'role' object below
POST _security/api_key                     <- { name, role_descriptors: { audit_service: <role> } }
Two properties matter most:
1. The service has NO 'delete' privilege on the audit data streams. Audit
records are append-only, and erasure is crypto-shredding, which touches
only the keyring index. Withholding 'delete' means a compromised service
credential cannot destroy audit evidence at all - the cluster refuses it,
rather than relying on the application never asking.
2. 'delete' IS granted on the keyring index, and only there. That single
deletion is the entire crypto-shredding mechanism, so it is the one
mutable surface the service needs.
manage_ilm and manage_index_templates are cluster-level because bootstrap
applies the ILM policy and index templates on startup. If policy is applied
out-of-band instead, drop both and the service still runs - it logs
cluster_bootstrap_failed and continues buffering.
'create_doc' allows indexing new documents but NOT overwriting an
existing one - the storage-layer expression of an append-only log.
'delete' and 'write' are deliberately absent: 'write' would permit
update and delete operations on audit records.
'manage' is needed for data stream rollover and point-in-time.
Backing indices (.ds-audit-*) must be listed: ILM and PIT address
them directly rather than through the data stream alias.
The one mutable store. 'delete' here is what executes a data-subject
erasure. It holds only WRAPPED data keys, so a stolen copy is still
gated by PII_MASTER_KEK, which lives outside the cluster.
Operationally this index is the single point of failure for PII
readability: lose it and every encrypted field is unreadable forever.
It must be included in the snapshot policy.

snapshot_policy_note: Elasticsearch is not the durability story for audit segments - the S3
Object Lock archive is. Snapshots still matter for two reasons:
1. audit-keyring-v1 exists ONLY in Elasticsearch. It is not archived,
because writing key material to WORM storage would make it
2. Restoring a cluster from the archive means replaying millions of
documents; a snapshot restore is hours faster.
The keyring must therefore be in a snapshot policy with a retention at
least as long as RETENTION_DAYS. A snapshot taken before an erasure will
still contain the destroyed key, so snapshot retention is itself a GDPR
consideration: keep it as short as the recovery objective allows, and
document the window in the DPIA.
